cause: The forward cargo door opened in flight because of faulty wiring and a deficient door latch design.
Fatigue cracking and bond failure in the fuselage lap joints went undetected because the airline's maintenance programme did not catch them.
The crew focused on a burned-out indicator bulb, stopped monitoring altitude and did not notice the descent.
The crew flew into a thunderstorm and met a microburst wind shear; training, procedures and hazard information were lacking.
The engine pylon was damaged by an improper maintenance procedure that used a forklift, and the engine separation cut hydraulics and slat warnings.
It ran out of fuel: the captain focused on the gear and did not heed the crew's fuel warnings.
A fatigue crack in the engine's fan disk, from a defect in the titanium, broke it apart and cut all three hydraulic systems.
Ice on the wings and the crew's failure to use engine anti-ice gave wrong thrust readings, and the takeoff was continued.
The NTSB found that the crew did not set the flaps and slats for takeoff, and the takeoff warning system did not sound.
The crew continued the approach in severe weather and the spoilers did not deploy after touchdown, so the aircraft could not stop.
The horizontal stabilizer trim jackscrew threads wore away because of inadequate maintenance and lubrication, and the assembly failed.

The NTSB found that freezing rain created an ice ridge beyond the de-icing boots, which caused the ailerons to snap and the autopilot to disconnect; ATR and the French authorities had not told operators enough about the risk.
The NTSB found that the captain responded incorrectly to the stick shaker stall warning, and that the crew had not monitored airspeed during the approach; fatigue and Colgan's procedures contributed.
The NTSB found that a bird strike by Canada geese damaged both engines beyond their ability to run; the crew's decisions and training contributed to the survival of everyone aboard.
The NTSB found that the crew mismanaged the approach and the autothrottle mode, and did not monitor airspeed, so the aircraft fell below the target speed and struck the seawall.
The crew did not use available cues to confirm the runway before takeoff and chatted during taxi; the FAA's lack of runway-crossing clearance rules contributed.
A fatigue crack in a fan blade dovetail let the blade separate and strike the engine inlet, breaking a window.
Mislabelled oxygen generators in the cargo hold set off a fire that the aircraft was not equipped to detect or put out.

incident: United Airlines Flight 585 / USAir Flight 427 / Eastwind Airlines Flight 517
cause: The 737 rudder power control unit could jam or move opposite to the pilot's command (rudder hardover), which was found to cause the crashes.
Flammable insulation materials let an in-flight fire spread beyond the crew's control, and the fire damaged the aircraft's systems.
After the pitot probes iced up and the autopilot disconnected, the crew did not recognise the stall and kept the nose up.
The windscreen was fitted with screws that were too small and too short, and could not hold against cabin pressure.
The crew shut down the wrong engine; the damaged one then failed, and a fan blade fatigue fault was the original cause.
The BEA concluded the co-pilot deliberately flew the aircraft into the terrain, while suffering from a mental disorder; the captain was locked out of the cockpit.
The MAX's flight control software (MCAS) relied on one angle-of-attack sensor that had been wrongly calibrated, and crew guidance and maintenance gaps contributed.
